This means that the crime-prevention measures have a beneficial influence beyond the places that they target, perhaps because offenders are not exactly sure where the crime-prevention measures have been introduced, which indicates that offenders are not likely to be local residents. 19 The main implication of the research studies above is that although improved street lighting might displace crime into nearby neighborhoods, it is just as likely to reduce crime in these neighborhoods because of a diffusion of benefits. 2.2.2.1.5 Reduced Street Lighting and Security There is to date no empirical evidence on whether the implementation of reduced street lighting has had any negative effects on these important public health outcomes. However, Steinbach’s study (Steinbach, 2015) did suggest an association between some street lighting adaptations and crime. The analysis included 581,837 burglaries, 475,657 thefts of or from a vehicle, 67,470 robberies, 486,367 criminal damage offences, and 730,280 violence offences between 2010 and 2013 across 62 local authority areas in England and Wales. While there was significant statistical heterogeneity in effects estimated at the police force level, results overall were suggestive of an association between dimming and reductions in crime, particularly for violent crime (Figure 10). These results may lend support to the hypothesis linking lower levels of visibility to difficulties in identifying “suitable” targets from those on the street at night. Estimates also provide suggestive evidence that part-night lighting may be associated with an increase in robbery. Results also suggested an association between white light and reductions in crime, particularly burglary, which may provide support for the credibility of mechanisms linking increased visibility or increased investment in local communities to reductions in crime. Again, as with the estimates of effects on safety, the absence of photometric details (such as illuminance or CCT) of adaptation strategies, especially the reduced lighting strategies at each region makes the conclusions questionable. 20 Figure 10. As an anecdotal example, leaving a porch light turned on can provide a feeling of security to a homeowner. 2.2.2.2.1 Street Lighting and Crime Public perception on street lightning and the relationship with crime, although it may not match the statistics on lighting and crime, reliably reflects the concern and fear. In Pain’s effort to qualify the effect of street lighting on crime and fear (Pain, 2006), local street lighting was viewed as problematic by a majority of residents in five of the ten study areas, regardless of the lighting coverage rating, meaning the geographical pattern of dissatisfaction does not correlate with the lighting coverage maps.
